mcq.q: What does a causal mask do?
options: Stops a token attending to later positions
mcq.why: It sets future scores to −∞ before softmax so each position sees only its prefix.

mcq.q: Encoder-only models such as BERT are trained to…
options: Fill in masked tokens, with every token seeing every other
mcq.why: Bidirectional attention suits understanding tasks: classification, extraction, embeddings and rerankers.
distractors: Speech models are a separate family.

mcq.q: Decoder-only models use which attention pattern?
options: Causal: each token sees only earlier tokens
mcq.why: They are trained to predict the next token, which suits generation.

mcq.q: Which family suits translation, summarisation and speech recognition, for example T5, BART and Whisper?
mcq.why: The encoder reads the input bidirectionally; the decoder generates with cross-attention to it.
distractors: Decoder-only models can do it, but these examples are encoder–decoder.
Encoders alone do not generate sequences.

mcq.q: You need fast sentence embeddings for vector search. Which architecture fits?
mcq.why: Most embedding models are encoders trained contrastively (4.4).
distractors: Chat models are slow and not trained for embeddings.

mcq.q: Why did decoder-only models win for general-purpose use?
options: One simple objective scales on any text, and every task can be phrased as continuation
mcq.why: Next-token prediction needs no labels and covers chat, code and agents.

mcq.q: In a RAG system, which three architectures commonly appear?
options: A bi-encoder for retrieval, a cross-encoder reranker, and a decoder-only answer model
Only a CNN and an RNN
mcq.why: Each transformer is matched to its job.
distractors: Decoders are a poor fit for fast retrieval and reranking.
That is not how RAG stacks are built.

mcq.q: How does a cross-encoder reranker differ from a bi-encoder?
options: It reads the query and passage together, which is more accurate but slower
mcq.why: A bi-encoder can precompute document vectors; a cross-encoder must run once per query–passage pair.
distractors: Answer generation is the decoder's job.

mcq.q: Whisper is an example of which architecture?
mcq.why: An audio encoder feeds a text decoder through cross-attention.
distractors: That is a different design dimension.
It generates text, so it has a decoder.

mcq.q: You mean-pool a generic encoder's outputs and use them as sentence embeddings without testing. What is the risk?
options: The result may be a poor sentence embedding; use a trained embedding model or evaluate first
mcq.why: Encoders not trained for similarity often give weak retrieval vectors.

interview.q: Compare encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder–decoder transformers.
What is the difference between a bi-encoder and a cross-encoder?
Why do decoder-only models dominate general-purpose AI?
Choose an architecture for each: classification, translation, chat, embeddings. Justify each choice.
{company} must classify dispute reasons into fixed labels. Would you use a fine-tuned encoder or a prompted LLM?
covers: Fixed labels and labelled data favour an encoder
LLM as a baseline or label bootstrapper
Compare on the same test set

interview.q: Why can adding a reranker improve RAG answers?
covers: Joint reading of query and passage

interview.q: Design a retrieve-rerank-generate stack with a latency budget.
covers: Bi-encoder or hybrid retrieval to top 50–100
interview.followUp: Where would you cut first if the budget halved?

interview.q: {company}'s search uses an LLM to rank every candidate product and is too slow. What would you change?
covers: Retrieve with embeddings or keywords first
Rerank a small set with a cross-encoder

mcq.q: Doubling context length roughly does what to attention compute?
mcq.why: Full attention compares every pair of tokens: cost grows with n².

mcq.q: In attention, what is the intuition behind query, key and value?
options: They are three copies of the same vector
Query: the user's question; key: the password; value: the answer
Query and key are the input and output tokens
Query: what I am looking for; key: what I contain; value: what I pass on
mcq.why: Each is a learned projection of the token's representation.
distractors: They come from different learned matrices.
These are internal vectors, not the user's question.
All three are computed for every token.

mcq.q: What is the attention formula?
mcq.why: Scores from query–key dot products are scaled, softmaxed, and used to average the values.
distractors: The softmax applies to the scores, not V.
That omits the transpose, scaling and softmax.
There is no softmax or scaling there.

mcq.q: Why divide attention scores by √d?
options: To keep scores in a range where softmax does not saturate
mcq.why: Dot products grow with dimension; scaling keeps the softmax from becoming nearly one-hot too early.
distractors: It does not change the speed.

mcq.q: What is cross-attention?
options: Queries come from one sequence (the decoder) and keys and values from another (the encoder output)
mcq.why: It lets a decoder look at the input sequence, as in translation.
distractors: Heads run in parallel; that is multi-head attention.
Future tokens are masked in generation.

mcq.q: What does multi-head attention do?
options: Attends only to the first token
Repeats the same attention several times
Runs several attentions in parallel with different projections, then concatenates them
mcq.why: Different heads can learn different relations, such as syntax or coreference.
distractors: Heads attend over all allowed tokens.
Each head has its own projections.

mcq.q: For a sequence of 1,000 tokens, how many query–key scores does one head compute?
mcq.why: Every query is compared with every key: 1,000 × 1,000. A causal mask hides about half, but they are still computed in a plain implementation.
distractors: That counts only the unmasked lower triangle including the diagonal.

mcq.q: A model has 32 attention heads, each of dimension 128. What is its model dimension?
mcq.why: 32 × 128 = 4,096, the d_model of an 8B-class model.

mcq.q: Engineers want to explain why an answer ignored a clause. What role should attention weights play?
options: They prove which document is true
One clue, alongside retrieval scores and the prompt, not a complete explanation
mcq.why: Attention shows where information flowed in one layer and head; many other computations shape the output.
distractors: They are not a complete account of behaviour.
They can still be a useful clue.

mcq.q: Each token's attention output is…
options: A copy of its own embedding
A weighted average of the value vectors
mcq.why: The weights come from how well its query matches each key.
distractors: Keys are used for scoring, not as the output.
Vocabulary probabilities come from the LM head.
Information is gathered from other tokens.

interview.q: Explain self-attention step by step.
covers: Project tokens to Q, K and V
Score every query against every key

interview.q: Why are attention scores scaled by √d?
What does multi-head attention add over a single head?
covers: Concatenate and mix with an output matrix
Same total size split across heads

interview.q: What does the n × n score matrix imply for long prompts?
covers: Compute grows with the square of length
FlashAttention avoids storing the full matrix

interview.q: An answer ignores a key clause in the retrieved text. How would you investigate, and where do attention weights fit?
covers: Check the clause was retrieved and in the prompt
Check its position and the prompt wording
Ablate: remove or move the clause and compare
interview.followUp: How would you turn the finding into a regression test?

interview.q: {assistant} sometimes links the wrong date to the wrong city in a long request. How would you reason about it, and what would you change?
covers: Attention can link distant words, but it is not guaranteed
Missing context such as today's date
Confirm key fields with the traveller

interview.q: Explain to a team why doubling the context more than doubles prefill cost, and how you would reduce it.
covers: Attention compute is quadratic in length

interview.q: How would you test whether a model actually uses a retrieved passage?
covers: Ablation: answer with and without it

mcq.q: An MoE model has 47B total and 13B active parameters. Memory for weights is driven by…
options: the number of experts used per token only
mcq.why: All experts must be resident, so weight memory follows total parameters.

mcq.q: In a dense model, which parameters are used for each token?
options: Only the experts the router picks
mcq.why: Dense models apply every weight to every token.

mcq.q: How does a mixture-of-experts layer work?
options: Experts are separate models called in sequence
A router picks the top few expert FFNs for each token, and their outputs are combined
mcq.why: For example, 2 of 8 or 8 of 128 experts per token.
distractors: That would be a large dense model.
They are inside each layer, chosen per token.
Experts replace the FFN, not attention.

mcq.q: Mixtral 8x7B has about 47B total and 13B active parameters. Its compute per token is roughly that of…
mcq.why: Only the active experts run per token, so compute follows active parameters while memory follows the total.
distractors: Each token uses two experts plus shared layers.
That is its memory footprint, not its compute.

mcq.q: What extra serving concern does MoE bring?
mcq.why: Uneven routing can overload some experts and GPUs (14.5).
distractors: They still have a KV cache.

mcq.q: How does the KV cache grow with context length?
mcq.why: One set of keys and values per token, per layer.
distractors: Attention compute is quadratic; the cache is linear.

mcq.q: For 32 layers, 8 KV heads of dimension 128 in BF16, how large is the KV cache per token?
mcq.why: 2 (K and V) × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes = 131,072 bytes = 128 KiB.
distractors: That forgets either K or V.
That is eight times too large.
That forgets the layer count's effect.

mcq.q: At 128 KiB per token, about how much KV cache does a 250,000-token prompt need?
mcq.why: 250,000 × 128 KiB ≈ 32 million KiB ≈ 30.5 GiB (about 33 GB).

mcq.q: What does FlashAttention change?
options: It makes attention linear in compute
It avoids storing the full n × n score matrix, though compute stays quadratic
mcq.why: It is a memory- and bandwidth-efficient kernel for the same computation.

mcq.q: Your documents fit in the context window. Why might stuffing them in still give worse answers?
options: Models use information in the middle of long contexts less reliably
mcq.why: “Fits in the window” does not mean “used well”; measure on your task.
distractors: Inputs within the limit are tokenised.

mcq.q: Retrieving the 5 most relevant chunks (about 3,000 tokens) instead of a 250,000-token manual is roughly how much cheaper in input tokens?
distractors: An order of magnitude too high.
An order of magnitude too low.

interview.q: Explain dense versus mixture-of-experts models and their trade-off.
covers: Dense uses all parameters per token
MoE routes tokens to a few experts

interview.q: Why does attention compute grow quadratically while the KV cache grows linearly?
covers: Every token compared with every other
One key and value per token per layer
Kernels avoid storing the n × n matrix
KV memory is often the serving limit

interview.q: What is the “lost in the middle” effect, and why does it matter?
covers: Long windows are not used uniformly
Measure by position on your task

interview.q: Should you put a 400-page manual in every prompt or retrieve from it? Argue with numbers.
covers: Seconds of prefill and about 31 GiB of KV cache
Prompt caching helps cost, not quality
interview.followUp: When would putting the whole document in context be the right call?

interview.q: How do you size the hardware for an MoE deployment?
covers: Compute per token from active parameters
KV cache for the expected context and concurrency

interview.q: At festival peak {company} expects 200 concurrent shoppers per GPU. How do context length choices affect that plan?
covers: KV cache per request times concurrency
About 4 GiB per 32k-token request for an 8B-class model

interview.q: Plan GPU memory for serving many concurrent long-context users.
covers: KV cache per token × context × concurrency
Paged KV cache and admission control (14.3)

interview.q: How would you evaluate whether a long-context model can replace your RAG pipeline?
covers: Task accuracy by position and length
Run both on the same evaluation set

mcq.q: Why do LLMs use subword tokenisation?
options: It makes every word one token
It removes the need for a vocabulary
It balances a fixed vocabulary against sequence length: common words stay whole, rare ones split
mcq.why: Whole words cannot cover typos and new names; single characters make sequences very long.
distractors: Subwords work for any language, unevenly.
Rare words split into several tokens.
There is still a fixed vocabulary.

mcq.q: How does Byte-Pair Encoding build its vocabulary?
options: Repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token
Assigns one token per dictionary word
mcq.why: Merges continue until the vocabulary reaches its target size; at tokenisation time they are applied in the same order.

mcq.q: In the corpus “hug hug pug pun bun”, which pair does BPE merge first?
mcq.why: Count adjacent pairs: u-g appears 3 times (hug, hug, pug); h-u, p-u and u-n appear twice each.

mcq.q: Why can byte-level BPE encode any text with no “unknown” token?
options: It translates text to English first
It starts from the 256 byte values, so every character can be built from bytes
It skips characters it does not know
mcq.why: Emoji and unseen scripts fall back to byte sequences.

mcq.q: Tokenizers are trained mostly on English-heavy data. What follows for other languages?
options: They often need more tokens for the same meaning: higher cost, slower replies and less room in context
mcq.why: Some scripts can need several times more tokens on older tokenizers.
distractors: They are processed, at a higher token cost.
Token count, cost and context use all change.

mcq.q: A support bot gives every conversation the same token budget. Why is that a fairness issue?
options: It removes the need for retrieval
Users of costlier languages get less history and retrieved context
mcq.why: The “token tax” means the same budget buys less content in some languages.

mcq.q: Why do models often fail to count the r's in “strawberry”?
options: They see tokens such as “str · aw · berry”, not individual letters
The vocabulary lacks the letter r
mcq.why: Character-level tasks should be done in code, with the LLM calling a tool (7.4).
distractors: They count tokens and items reasonably; characters are the problem.
Letters are in the vocabulary; the word is not split that way.

mcq.q: What do newer models' larger vocabularies (100k–260k tokens) do to the multilingual gap?
options: Reduce it, but not eliminate it
mcq.why: Always measure token counts on your real languages before estimating cost.

mcq.q: You estimate Tamil support costs from English token counts. What is likely to happen?
options: You underestimate cost and overestimate how much fits in context
mcq.why: Tamil text usually needs more tokens than English for the same meaning.
distractors: It can be tokenised, at more tokens.
The error usually goes the other way.

mcq.q: How do WordPiece and Unigram (SentencePiece) tokenizers differ from BPE?
options: They are used only for images
They do not use a vocabulary
They choose merges or pieces differently but have the same effect: a subword vocabulary
mcq.why: All three produce subword vocabularies; the selection criterion differs.

interview.q: How does BPE tokenisation work?
covers: Count adjacent pairs and merge the most frequent
Repeat to a target vocabulary size
Apply the merges in order at tokenisation time

interview.q: Why do non-English languages often cost more tokens, and why does it matter?
covers: More tokens for the same meaning
Higher cost and latency, less context

interview.q: Why do LLMs struggle to count letters or reverse strings?
covers: Let the model call a tool

interview.q: How would you estimate token costs for a multilingual assistant?
covers: Count with the model's own tokenizer
Weight by the language mix and monitor it
interview.followUp: What would you do if one language turned out three times more expensive?

interview.q: Your chunker budgets by words and sometimes splits order IDs. What goes wrong, and how do you fix it?
covers: Split IDs break exact matching and citations
Never split inside identifiers or table rows

interview.q: {assistant} serves four languages with one fixed token budget per conversation. Is that fair, and what would you change?
covers: Fixed budgets give costlier languages less context
Budget by meaning or per language

interview.q: Design a token-budgeting service for a multilingual assistant.
covers: Count with each model's tokenizer at runtime
Reserves for system prompt and output
Priority rules for history and retrieved text
Per-language monitoring of cost and truncation
Alerts when budgets cut context often

interview.q: Design how {company}'s assistant handles transaction references and amounts so tokenisation can never corrupt them.
covers: Identifiers and amounts come from records, inserted by code
The model refers to placeholders, not raw values
Validation of every identifier in the output

mcq.q: Why does a transformer need positional information?
options: Attention alone treats the input as a set, so shuffling tokens shuffles outputs the same way
mcq.why: Word order must be injected, for example with RoPE or position embeddings.
distractors: It is about order, not speed.

mcq.q: What does RoPE (rotary position embedding) do?
options: Adds a learned vector to each token
Rotates queries and keys by angles proportional to position, so their dot product depends on relative distance
mcq.why: The score between positions m and n depends on m − n.

mcq.q: What does a residual connection compute?
mcq.why: Adding the input back gives gradients a direct path through many layers.
distractors: Residuals add, they do not multiply.

mcq.q: What does “pre-norm” mean in modern LLM blocks?
mcq.why: RMSNorm before attention and before the FFN is common.
distractors: Data normalisation is a different step.
The final norm is only one of them.

mcq.q: How is the feed-forward network applied in a transformer block?
options: To each position independently: expand, non-linearity, project back
mcq.why: It typically widens the vector about 3.5–4× and often uses SwiGLU.
distractors: Mixing across positions is attention's job.

mcq.q: Roughly what share of a dense model's parameters sit in its feed-forward layers?
mcq.why: FFNs are thought to store much of the model's factual associations.
distractors: Attention and embeddings hold the rest.

mcq.q: A SwiGLU FFN has 3 matrices of 4,096 × 14,336. About how many parameters is that per layer?
distractors: That is ten times too many.

mcq.q: In an 8B-class model with vocabulary 128,256 and d = 4,096, about how many parameters are the input and output embeddings together?
mcq.why: 2 × 128,256 × 4,096 ≈ 1.05B, on top of about 7.0B in the 32 layers.
distractors: That uses only part of the vocabulary.

mcq.q: With grouped-query attention (d = 4,096, 8 KV heads of 128), Q and O are 4,096 × 4,096 and K and V are 4,096 × 1,024. About how many attention parameters are in one layer?
distractors: That treats K and V as full 4,096 × 4,096.
That counts only K and V.

mcq.q: A provider advertises a 1M-token context, but accuracy falls for facts placed mid-context beyond about 60k tokens. What should you conclude?
options: A configured length is not evidence the model was trained or evaluated to use it well
mcq.why: Measure use of the window on your own task before relying on it.
distractors: They can work; measure on your task.
Evidence shows it is not used well.
The window exists; quality across it varies.

interview.q: Describe the anatomy of one transformer block.
covers: Repeated L times, then final norm and LM head

interview.q: Why do residual connections matter?
covers: Blocks write into a shared stream

interview.q: Explain RoPE and why most current LLMs use it.
covers: Rotates Q and K by position

interview.q: Count the parameters of an 8B-class model from its shape.
interview.followUp: How does tying the input and output embeddings change the total?

interview.q: A model card says 128k context. How do you decide how much of it to use?
covers: Test recall at different positions and lengths
Measure task quality, not just fit
Cost and latency per extra token

interview.q: {company}'s shopper chats grow long during comparisons. How would you manage the context?
Estimate the memory and compute needed to serve a given model shape.
covers: Weights from parameter count and precision
KV cache per token from layers, KV heads and head dimension

interview.q: A vendor extends a model's context window after training. What changes, and how would you validate it?
covers: RoPE scaling or similar plus long-context fine-tuning
Needle and multi-fact tests by position
Task evaluation at your real lengths
Latency and cost at long contexts

mcq.q: What are logits?
options: Raw, unbounded scores the LM head outputs, one per vocabulary token
mcq.why: Softmax turns them into probabilities.

mcq.q: Logits [2.0, 1.0, 0.1] go through softmax. What are the probabilities, roughly?
distractors: That divides logits by their sum instead of exponentiating.

mcq.q: With those probabilities, the true next token is the second one. What is the cross-entropy loss?
distractors: That is the probability, not the loss.

mcq.q: What happens if you add the same constant to every logit?
options: Nothing: softmax depends only on the differences
mcq.why: The constant cancels in the ratio.

mcq.q: Three logits are all equal to 1. What probability does each token get?
mcq.why: Equal logits give a uniform distribution.
distractors: That is the exponential before normalising.

mcq.q: Why is generation inherently sequential?
options: Each output token becomes part of the input for the next step
mcq.why: Token 50 cannot be computed before token 49.
distractors: Vocabulary size is not the reason.

mcq.q: What is the difference between prefill and decode?
options: Prefill processes the whole prompt in one parallel pass; decode produces one token per pass
Prefill writes the answer; decode reads the prompt
mcq.why: Prefill is fast per token; decode is slow per token.
distractors: They differ in parallelism and cost.

mcq.q: What does the KV cache store?
options: Keys and values for earlier tokens, so they are not recomputed each step
mcq.why: Without it every decode step would recompute the whole prefix (14.1).

mcq.q: An assistant streams its answer: the first words appear after about 0.7 s and the full answer after 4 s. What does streaming improve?
options: Perceived latency (time to first token), not total generation time
mcq.why: Users see progress sooner; the same number of tokens is still generated.

mcq.q: A sentence's first token had probability 0.9. What does that say about the sentence's factual correctness?
options: Nothing reliable: a likely next token is not evidence the whole sentence is true
It is 90% likely to be correct
mcq.why: Probability measures likely continuation, not truth (1.3).
distractors: Token probability is not factual confidence.

interview.q: Explain logits, softmax and how the next token is chosen.
covers: A decoding rule picks a token (5.6)

interview.q: Why is autoregressive generation sequential, and what does that mean for latency?
covers: Each token depends on the previous ones
One forward pass per output token

interview.q: What are prefill and decode, and what is the KV cache for?
covers: Cache of past keys and values

interview.q: Users say the assistant is slow. How do you tell whether prefill or decode is the problem?
covers: Measure time to first token versus time between tokens
Fix with shorter prompts, caching or output limits
interview.followUp: Which metric would you put on the dashboard?

interview.q: Why does streaming improve perceived latency, and what does it not fix?
{company}'s assistant explains refund decisions. Why should the decision not be streamed as it is generated?
covers: Compute values in code, then phrase
Stream only the explanation around validated values

interview.q: Design a generation flow where numbers come from tools while the text streams.
covers: Call tools before or alongside generation
Hold lines with numbers until verified

interview.q: Estimate end-to-end latency from prompt size, output size and hardware.
covers: Prefill tokens per second for the prompt
Decode tokens per second for the output

mcq.q: What does greedy decoding do?
options: Always takes the most probable token
mcq.why: It is deterministic in principle and can be repetitive.

mcq.q: What does a temperature below 1 do?
options: Sharpens the distribution, making output more predictable
mcq.why: Logits are divided by T before softmax; T < 1 exaggerates differences.

mcq.q: Logits are [2, 0]. At temperature 2, what is the first token's probability?
mcq.why: Divide by T: [1, 0]. softmax gives e/(e + 1) ≈ 0.73, lower than 0.88 at T = 1.

mcq.q: What does top-k sampling do?
options: Keeps tokens with probability above k
Keeps only the k most probable tokens, renormalises and samples
mcq.why: It removes the long tail of unlikely tokens.
distractors: One token is sampled per step.

mcq.q: What does top-p (nucleus) sampling do?
options: Keeps tokens with probability above p
Keeps the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p
mcq.why: The set adapts to how confident the model is.
distractors: It is cumulative, not a per-token threshold.

mcq.q: Probabilities are [0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.05]. With top-p = 0.8, which tokens are kept?
mcq.why: 0.5 + 0.3 = 0.8 reaches p, so the nucleus is the top two.
distractors: The third is not needed to reach 0.8.

mcq.q: Why should you always set a maximum number of new tokens?
options: It is required by every tokenizer
mcq.why: Without it, a runaway generation can cost a lot and take a long time.

mcq.q: With temperature 0 and a fixed seed, outputs still differ between runs. Which is a valid cause?
options: Floating-point order on GPUs, batching, hardware or library differences, or a silent model update
The seed is ignored on Tuesdays
mcq.why: Tiny numeric differences can flip a near-tie, and the texts then diverge.
distractors: Temperature 0 is the least random setting.
That is not a real cause.

mcq.q: How should tests for LLM output be written, given non-determinism?
options: Run once and trust the result
Check properties, such as valid JSON or a required clause, and pin model versions
mcq.why: Property checks survive harmless wording changes.
distractors: Exact strings fail on harmless variation.

mcq.q: Which settings suit extracting data into JSON?
options: Temperature 0, a constrained schema and a token limit
mcq.why: Extraction needs predictable, valid output.
distractors: Variety is the opposite of what extraction needs.

interview.q: Explain temperature, top-k and top-p.
covers: Order of filters varies by engine

interview.q: Why is temperature 0 not a guarantee of identical outputs?
What stop conditions should every generation have?
Pick decoding settings for extraction, reply drafting and brainstorming, and justify them.
Your regression tests started failing after a provider update, though answers look fine. What happened, and what do you change?
covers: Model version or batching changed wording
interview.followUp: Which properties would you check for a customer reply?

interview.q: {company} extracts attributes from seller descriptions and also writes product copy. Which settings for each, and why?
Design an evaluation harness that is robust to non-determinism.
covers: Pinned model versions and seeds where possible

interview.q: The same decoding settings behave differently on two providers. Why, and what do you do?
covers: Tune per provider and compare on your evaluation set
